data.title: A protected life is not yet a full one
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Jeffery Tan’s commentary “In a super-aged Singapore society, we must learn to differentiate independence from dignity” on Sep 19 made an argument that Singapore’s ageing debate badly needs: Independence and dignity are not the same thing. Independence may diminish, but dignity should not follow.

He is right about the mechanism, too.

Care can turn into control gradually, through a sequence of individually sensible decisions – a child takes over the appointments, a helper decides the bath time – until “a life gets organised around a person without being lived with them”, as he put it. 

Nobody intends it. Everybody is being reasonable.

I want to carry his argument one step further, because I think it stops just short of where it is going.

Consider what the instruments mentioned in his commentary actually do. A Lasting Power of Attorney, an Advance Medical Directive, Advance Care Planning, the discipline of offering choices that are real rather than token: These are good things, and far too few families use them. 

But they protect just two things – the older person’s autonomy, and their security. They settle who decides, and they keep the person safe.

That is a floor. It is not a room.

Seven domains, but only two funded

American geriatrician G Allen Power, working with people living with dementia, builds his case on a seven-domain model of well-being developed by the non-profit organisation Eden Alternative: identity, connectedness, security, autonomy, meaning, growth and joy.

Set that list against our care system, and the asymmetry is immediate. Society has instruments for security and autonomy – legal, clinical, procedural, auditable. For the other five, there is almost nothing.

No care plan in Singapore asks whether a person still has an identity beyond “patient” or “resident”. None asks whether anyone in the building knows what they were good at, or who they were at 40. None asks what they are still learning. None asks when they last laughed at something.

Our licence conditions for nursing homes are precise about safety: fall risk reassessed every six months, skin inspected daily, every medication error documented and reviewed, nutritional status screened. Quite right. 

They also require psychosocial assessment and meaningful activities, but name no instrument, no interval and no threshold. A home can meet every requirement in that document, and still be a place where people have nothing to look forward to.

This is not for want of measurement instruments. In a 2021 study I conducted with other academics, we measured psychosocial qualities directly in 696 residents in seven Singapore nursing homes: quality of life, well-being observed minute by minute, and the level of person-centred care each home achieved.

Person-centred care in the homes scored 2.3 out of 4. Resident satisfaction was 3.43 out of 5, lowest of all on lifestyle and the quality of interaction.

And the homes scoring higher on person-centred care had residents who were measurably better off.

The assessment tools exist; they have been validated in our study of nursing homes in Singapore, yet they form no part of how anyone is held to account.

Growth is the domain society finds hardest to take seriously. It is assumed to belong to the first half of life, that after a certain point, a person is maintained rather than developed. 

Yet, the people I meet in their 80s who feel most alive are almost always learning something: a language, an instrument badly, their great-grandchildren’s names and politics. 

Nothing in Singapore’s system of care has a place to record this, and so nothing in it is organised to make it possible.

Why society does not ask

Part of the reason is that society has quietly made enjoyment conditional.

Pleasure in the later parts of life gets justified by what it does for health: Singing is good for the lungs, friendship is good for cognition, gardening counts as exercise. The activity has to earn its place by its health dividend.

This instinct has a name: healthism. It has a weaker evidential basis than most people assume.

In another study I co-authored, we followed a cohort of 6,073 older Singaporeans for nearly 12 years, and found that happiness predicted survival, until health and psychological functioning were accounted for, at which point the association disappeared. 

We gave the paper the title the data deserved: Happy people live longer because they are healthy people.

Enjoyment does not have to buy its keep by extending life. It has value in itself. And once that is clear, something else follows; the pleasures of later life need no justification, beyond being good.

A hot drink taken slowly. A room where someone uses your name. Being asked for a recipe that only you still remember.

For a person whose capacity is genuinely diminishing, these are not consolations for the life that has been lost. They are life itself.

What this asks of society are modest and specific. When a family is choosing a care arrangement, the question to ask on the visit is not only what is prevented, but also what a good day looks like here. 

When a board or investor looks at a care operator, the quality dashboard will be composed almost entirely of safety measures – ask what sits beside them. 

In July 2026, the Ministry of Health’s deputy director-general of health regulation, Dr Raymond Chua, said a public rating system for nursing homes was worth studying.

If one comes, the question it must settle is whether it counts only what is prevented, or also what a resident’s day contains. For instance, Australia publishes what residents themselves say.

And it is not a trade-off between psychosocial satisfaction and running a good operation. When one Singapore home for residents with dementia rebuilt its care around the resident rather than the routine, well-being improved measurably, withdrawal and passive engagement fell, and staff attrition dropped by 55 per cent.

When Singapore builds on the support for ageing people that Tan mentioned in his article – the Agency for Integrated Care, Dementia Singapore, the Caregivers Alliance – it should be remembered that the circle is also made of unofficial things: a choir, a fishing trip, a weekly breakfast, the neighbour who still drops by.

As he wrote: “Someone who can no longer manage money or walk unaided may still... ask for a familiar visitor.”

These are not the soft edges of care. For five of the seven domains, they are the whole of it.

Tan ends with a line worth keeping in mind: Good care is not taking someone safely to a destination others have chosen for them, it is helping them stay part of the journey. That is exactly right. 

But staying part of the journey is the minimum they are owed. The harder question, and the one society has not begun to fund, is what is on the journey that makes it worth staying for.

The writer is an associate professor at the S R Nathan School of Human Development, Singapore University of Social Sciences. He has researched ageing in Singapore for two decades, and is the editor of a forthcoming volume on ageing in Asia.

data.title: Hyundai Elexio review: The Korean EV built for Chinese tastes
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Hyundai Elexio has a secret under its floor: Its battery pack is full of BYD Blade cells, which have a reputation here for not turning the cars above them into fiery deathtraps. I never said it was an exciting secret.

Still, it makes the Elexio an unusual creature. Conceived by Beijing Hyundai, it’s a Korean electric vehicle built in China, very much for Chinese tastes.

Those tastes are obvious the moment you climb in. Across the dashboard runs a 27-inch touchscreen (made up of one seamless pane rather than two abutting screens), which looks expensive enough to have annoyed the killjoys in charge of cost control at Beijing Hyundai.

Physical buttons, apart from those on the steering wheel, number somewhere around zero – a departure from the button-and-knob user-friendliness of the other Hyundai EVs.

As much as I’ve come to detest touchscreens, the Elexio’s is at least whimsical. You can set the home screen as a 3D cityscape with buildings that represent apps. Want to engage Apple CarPlay? Fly into the tower with the relevant logo on top.

There are also arcade games to let you while away the time if you’re waiting for the car to finish charging. My favourite is a racing game that you can play using the steering wheel and pedals, which tickled me more than it should a grown man.

Adjusting the air-conditioning or seat ventilation on the move takes too many taps, but on the plus side, the Elexio has a slim display at the base of the windscreen, much like the new BMW iX3’s. It’s bright, clear and puts important info such as your speed in your eyeline.

In other places, the cabin smacks of effort. The materials are soft to the touch and feel posh (more grief for Mr Cost Controller and gang), and overall the interior feels plusher than, say, the inside of a Mercedes-Benz GLB.

Rear passengers get air-con vents in the pillars, there are enough cupholders to satisfy a serious Chagee junkie, and the backrests recline enough to put some airline seats to shame (admittedly, not hard to do).

A companion smartphone app, the kind that lets you pre-cool the cabin before stepping in, would have been nice to have, especially since plenty of Chinese EVs at this price have one, but the Elexio is otherwise a practical machine.

The boot holds 506 litres, or 1,540 l with the seats folded. There’s no frunk, which is surprising given that there isn’t exactly a nuclear reactor under the bonnet.

Instead, the Elexio has a 136-horsepower motor that hauls the car along pretty gamely but, ultimately, pretty languidly – zero to 100 kmh takes all of 10.7 seconds.

What I disliked most behind the wheel is that there’s a lag between pressing the accelerator and anything happening when you pull away, which makes you feel like your trousers are around your ankles when you’re trying to win a traffic-light Grand Prix.

Yet, the chassis is a delight. The Elexio corners with real poise, barely rolls, and the steering tells you what the front tyres are up to, which isn’t a given with Chinese EVs.

In fact, it feels slightly sharper than Hyundai’s own Ioniq 5, although really, the gentle acceleration means it’s just best to leave it in the Eco driving mode and enjoy the scenery.

You can do that for up to 405 km in the Standard Range version I tried. The Long Range version (which costs S$24,000 more) stretches that to 546 km, but carrying nearly 300 kg more, it needs 12.1 seconds to reach 100 kmh.

For S$191,999 with Certificate Of Entitlement (COE), the Standard Range is the one to have, if you ask me, especially if the majority of your motoring is confined to Singapore.

Come to think of it, as much as the Elexio was aimed at China (Hyundai doesn’t even sell it in South Korea), it might as well have been built to Singaporean tastes. It’s roomy, pleasingly plush inside and priced like a Chinese car, though it steers more sweetly than one.

It also has those BYD Blade battery cells, which can only be a selling point, given how much BYD has earned the trust of buyers here. For the Elexio, they may turn out to be not so much a secret as a secret weapon.

data.title: Bringing independent directors into the family boardroom without losing trust
data.description:
FOR many closely held enterprises across Singapore and South-east Asia, inviting non-family directors into the boardroom can feel like sharing the family keys.

It is not that the value of independent perspectives is not recognised. The real challenge is introducing new capabilities without undermining the trusted advisers, family friends and confidants who may have helped build the business.

This concern is a deeply understandable sentiment, and one rooted in genuine pride of ownership.

Yet today, that traditional approach faces an unprecedented inflection point. Across South-east Asia, a vast cohort of family enterprises is preparing for handovers in both ownership and leadership.

Data from HSBC’s global private banking unit indicates that roughly 85 per cent of Asian family owned enterprises will execute a wealth and leadership transfer within the next decade.

At the same time, even as public regulators such as the Singapore Exchange Regulation have progressively raised board-independence standards for listed companies, many middle-market private family firms continue to operate without independent board representation.

As these businesses actively pursue regional expansion, strategic diversification and international capital, not all have established formal non-family oversight equipped to support that cross-border complexity.

The agile, relationship-driven approach of the founding generation worked brilliantly to build these businesses.

However, as ownership becomes increasingly dispersed across generations, operations span multiple jurisdictions, and external capital partners seek greater transparency, informal governance structures are tested in entirely new ways.

Tipping points driving governance reform

In our advisory work with multigenerational family enterprises across the region, we consistently observe four operational crossroads where traditional governance structures reach their limit.

The first involves navigating strategic blind spots. Relying exclusively on internal perspectives over long horizons can naturally narrow a firm’s strategic lens.

For example, as Singapore-based property titans expand internationally, integrating seasoned independent directors with cross-border experience provides essential objectivity when evaluating complex overseas assets.

The second crossroads is the emotional and relational weight of leadership succession. Handovers test family alignment like few other events.

High-profile succession challenges across the region offer a quiet reminder of what can happen when a business lacks neutral arbiters: sensitive family discussions can quickly blur into commercial friction, threatening both value and enterprise reputation.

Independent directors serve as essential shock absorbers, helping depersonalise difficult choices and establishing clear, objective rules of engagement.

Third is the sheer arithmetic of a growing family tree. By the third or fourth generation, balancing diverse family expectations with commercial realities becomes a delicate exercise.

Transitioning to a structured board creates a clear operational boundary, allowing the enterprise to run as a disciplined commercial entity while giving family diplomacy its own dedicated space.

Finally, there is the rising expectation from external capital. Lenders, institutional co-investors, and credit-rating agencies increasingly look for structured oversight.

Singapore’s listed-company governance framework has raised expectations for board independence, creating a benchmark that private firms may increasingly need to consider when seeking sophisticated global growth capital.

Evolving the board while building trust

Welcoming non-family directors does not mean surrendering family control or compromising core values. Instead, it requires a clear playbook built on shared intention rather than rigid corporate formulas.

To start, families should design a board tailored strictly to their strategic priorities, rather than adopting a generic template.

If the next five years are focused on professionalising operations or executing cross-border acquisitions, the board should recruit directors who bring direct, hands-on experience in those exact domains.

Crucially, this evolution does not need to happen overnight; governance is a gradual process of building trust. Board evolution in a family enterprise is rarely a clean-sheet exercise and, often, the most practical route to a stronger board is to add before you subtract.

Consider the example of a second-generation CEO who inherited a board comprising longstanding family friends. While their decades of loyalty carried immense emotional weight, the business had grown significantly more complex.

Simply asking these directors to step down was culturally non-viable and would have felt like a rejection of the relationships that built the firm. Instead, the CEO expanded the board to introduce independent directors with contemporary capabilities, thoughtfully shifting the boardroom dynamic over time without dishonouring historical contributions.

Furthermore, introducing independent perspectives is not about replacing family judgment, but ensuring family judgment is fully informed.

In another family enterprise we worked with, family members occupied several board seats and possessed an intimate understanding of the business. However, some had grown far removed from shifting competitive dynamics, technology shifts and market trends. Board discussions increasingly leaned on historical precedent rather than current data.

By introducing independent directors, the firm brought fresh discipline to the conversation. Assumptions were constructively tested, external benchmarks were introduced, and strategic proposals were backed by market evidence.

Far from diminishing the family’s role, the move allowed family directors to focus on what they do best – stewarding the company’s heritage, values and long-term vision – while grounding every strategic decision in contemporary market reality.

Cultural alignment and emotional intelligence (EI) are non-negotiable qualities that independent directors must have. Technical capability is merely the baseline. They must possess genuine empathy and a deep respect for the family’s legacy, culture and risk tolerance. An adviser lacking high EI may misread subtle family dynamics and fracture trust when sensitive topics arise.

Finally, successful leaders establish clear boundaries between enterprise governance and family governance. Fiduciary boards function best when kept clear of domestic disagreements.

Establishing parallel structures, such as family councils or assemblies, to oversee dividend policies, family charters and next-generation development allows boardroom discussions to remain focused squarely on business strategy and performance.

Preserving legacy through rigour

Inviting independent directors into the inner circle is not a retreat from family stewardship; done thoughtfully, it is one of its highest expressions.

Objective board members bring the candour, market insight and constructive challenge required to navigate an unpredictable global environment, fostering greater resilience.

For family business leaders across South-east Asia, the key question to confront now is whether informal governance has the structural strength and adaptability to support where the family wants to go next.

The writer is Singapore country manager at Russell Reynolds Associates

data.title: Cabin fever: Airlines are rushing to refurbish plane interiors, but will their bets pay off?
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore Airlines (SIA) will soon pull the cover off its highly anticipated next-generation cabin products, which are part of its S$1.1 billion retrofit programme for 41 aircraft.

The launch is in line with a broader industry overhaul – what airline reviewer Aaron Wong, who runs travel hacks website The MileLion, describes as an “aviation arms race”.

SIA aside, Emirates, All Nippon Airways (ANA), Cathay Pacific and other airlines have also embarked on or announced makeovers for their aircraft interiors in recent years. Some carriers are splashing out as much as US$7 billion on modern features and cutting-edge technology.

But does a facelift really help to improve airlines’ competitiveness? Is the retrofit worth the hefty investment and opportunity cost – and will customers see fares rise as a result?

Longer lifespans

Since a cabin has a commercial life of roughly seven to 10 years, and a plane’s airframe lasts 20 to 25 years, “refurbishment closes that gap” in the lifespan of airlines’ core assets, Linus Bauer, founder of aviation consultancy BAA & Partners, says.

Emirates’ ongoing cabin modernisation, announced in late 2021, is the largest such push in the aviation industry.

“It reflects our philosophy of continuously investing in the customer experience rather than waiting for a product to become outdated,” a spokesperson says.

Emirates has retrofitted 107 aircraft as at early October, with another 112 to go. Factors that go into when and whether to retrofit a plane include aircraft age, business strategy for the overall fleet, technological advancements, and customer expectations, the spokesperson adds.

Bauer observes that networkwide consistency in cabin products is another important driver for refurbishment, because “a brand promise is only as strong as the oldest aircraft on the network”.

That’s as DBS analyst Jason Sum notes that seats, entertainment systems and cabin design can become dated much more quickly – a trend that The MileLion’s Wong attributes to travellers’ increasing demands, such as the expectation of state-of-the-art conveniences.

For instance, passengers who get used to the high-speed Internet provided by SpaceX’s Starlink satellites could go out of their way to book flights with Starlink connections on board.

“It’s very hard to go back to a non-Starlink flight because it’s just night and day,” Wong muses.

Keeping up with peers

Cabin refurbishment can also be driven by changes in passenger preferences, Sum says.

For example, premium cabins have become increasingly important, particularly on long-haul routes, so airlines may use refurbishment programmes to introduce newer business-class seats, premium economy, improved entertainment systems and better connectivity.

Concurring, Bauer believes it gives the airlines a chance to increase the percentage of premium economy seats in their planes amid robust demand for that category.

Emirates introduced a new premium economy cabin during its retrofit, with 3,800 seats in this between-business-and-economy class installed to date.

But Dr Jeffrey Goh, managing director at Alton Aviation Consultancy, argues that airlines do not often use refurbishment to reconfigure layouts and replace economy seats with premium seats.

Such a move “must be aligned with the nature of the market in which the airline operates and hence its demand dynamics”, says Dr Goh, a veteran of aviation network Star Alliance who served as its CEO from 2017 to 2022 before running Gulf Air Group until October 2025.

He says: “This is a strategic matter that takes into account the airline’s current and future network, fleet, customer segments and travel trends in order to optimise revenue.”

ANA will be refreshing its business class seats for mid-sized aircraft for the first time in a decade with the addition of privacy doors on its long-haul Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner fleet from 2026.

Still, fleet configurations are determined by internal route-by-route yield evaluations and capacity planning, even as the industry shifts towards premium cabins, its spokesperson says.

While airlines invest in cabins to reinforce their brand appeal and competitiveness, industry observers note that the edge will be blunted as peers similarly upgrade their own products.

When it’s the first to market, a materially better cabin can strengthen customer preference, DBS’ Sum notes – particularly among premium passengers. But as peers give theirs a facelift as well, the benefit shifts from differentiation towards maintaining product parity.

Bauer says: “You run to stay in place. A refurbishment rarely creates a lasting advantage. Not refurbishing, however, creates a lasting disadvantage.”

Ultimately, the aviation industry is highly competitive, with customers choosing an airline based on their overall experience – not just cabin products, but passenger service, lounge offerings, entertainment, connectivity, network and reliability as well, Emirates’ spokesperson notes.

“Airlines will continue to invest in their products, just as we will continue to innovate and evolve ours. But our focus remains on continuously raising the bar for the overall customer experience rather than comparing any single feature against our peers,” the spokesperson adds.

Does the price tag pay off?

Cabin refurbishment does not come cheap.

Cathay Pacific in August 2026 committed HK$150 billion (US$19.1 billion) in investments for its fleet, cabin and lounge products, and digital innovation, according to Aldric Chau, regional general manager for South-east Asia and Oceania, though he did not give a breakdown for each category.

Upcoming refurbishments at the Hong Kong carrier include new business class seats for regional routes on selected Airbus A330s, and enhancements to its Airbus A321neo cabins.

Globally, the aircraft refurbishing market is projected to grow by an annual average of 5.1 per cent to hit US$9.7 billion in 2036, according to market research company Fact.MR.

But the spending can make sense for airlines, DBS’ Sum says – particularly for aircraft that still have many years of useful life remaining. Refurbishment is considerably cheaper than acquiring a new aircraft, and allows airlines to extend the commercial relevance of their existing fleet.

“The most direct return should come through higher yields, particularly if an improved cabin allows the airline to attract more premium passengers or reduce discounting versus competitors,” he says.

“Beyond that, refurbishment can also support customer loyalty, repeat business and brand perception, but these benefits are much harder to measure and quantify.”

If returns on investment are measured by revenue per seat and per flight, upsell conversion, share of corporate travel won, and satisfaction and loyalty, Bauer says: “A premium-heavy retrofit on an aircraft with a decade of life left can typically pay back within a few years.”

Yet Sum notes that there is also an opportunity cost, especially during periods where demand is robust, because aircraft have to be taken out of service during modification.

While refurbishment or retrofitting is generally scheduled in tandem with a major aircraft check to minimise disruption to aircraft utilisation, Dr Goh says that is not always possible, as the available timeslots may not be aligned.

At Emirates, which usually refreshes two to three aircraft a month out of its Dubai hangars, a Boeing 777 aircraft requires an average of 18 days to refurbish, while an Airbus A380 takes 22 days. Altogether, it took about 4.4 million people-hours to complete the retrofit of Emirates’ first 100 aircraft.

The good news is that travellers may not necessarily have to fork out more for a comfier flight, as the bill for cabin rejuvenation may not translate to higher ticket prices.

“Fare price movements are subject to the market environment and competition,” says Dr Goh. “Financing refurbishments is not necessarily (solely) dependent on future revenue. It may be financed by reserves that an airline has carefully planned over the years. Or a combination of both.”

Emirates’ spokesperson says that refurbishment does not have a direct impact on fares, while the ANA spokesperson tells The Business Times that airfares depend on a complex mix of market demand, seasonality, and broader economic conditions, rather than just hardware upgrades.

Still, Lorraine Tan, director of Asian equity research at Morningstar, does not expect the roll-out of fancy new cabin products to bump up ticket prices.

That’s as the airline business must strike a balance between load factor and yields. “If load factors start to slip because of competition, we think fares are unlikely to rise,” she says.

Instead, airlines monetise refurbishment more subtly, Bauer of BAA & Partners says: “They sell a better cabin mix, convert economy passengers into premium economy (ones), strengthen corporate deals and defend premium yields.”

As ANA’s spokesperson puts it: “While ticket prices are not directly pegged to cabin retrofits, investment in enhanced product features increases overall passenger perceived value, which naturally aligns with market willingness to pay for premium experiences.”

But The MileLion’s Wong cautions that airlines may be more restrictive about frequent flyer mileage redemptions when they release new cabin products.

He has seen “quite a few airlines” either block off lower-tier redemptions or completely disallow redemptions altogether after launching “nice new seats”, he tells BT.

“I understand that airlines always have a tendency, understandably, to prioritise commercial passengers – the ones paying cash – as opposed to the ones redeeming miles.”

Upgrades to continue

Refurbishing ageing cabins makes sense in light of an industrywide shortage of new planes. Airbus and Boeing delivered roughly 1,400 aircraft in all in 2025, even as more than 3,500 of the in-service planes built by these two titans were at least 20 years old.

But might cabin refreshment fall by the wayside when manufacturers ramp-up the delivery of new aircraft?

Perhaps not.

Though the supply of new aircraft may have some impact on the rate of refurbishment demand, there will always be planes in operation that require it, says Dr Goh.

It is unlikely that the rate of new aircraft deliveries will be able to replace older aircraft in operation, so there will likely be some sort of refurbishment still ongoing, says the consultant, who has a PhD in airline competition and regulation.

Indeed, the ANA spokesperson tells BT that refurbishment cycles depend on aircraft usage, maintenance schedules, technology evolution, and changing market expectations.

The airline periodically updates its cabin interiors to ensure safety, functional efficiency, and modern customer comfort throughout each aircraft’s operational life.

Meanwhile, Emirates’ spokesperson says that the carrier’s retrofitting efforts and new aircraft deliveries are designed to be complementary, as both programmes are important components of its long-term fleet and customer experience strategy.

The buzz around cabin refreshment is unlikely to taper off soon, according to watchers who highlight the years-long backlog in aircraft deliveries from Airbus and Boeing.

Sum from DBS notes that the production of widebody aircraft remains significantly below pre-pandemic levels, even as narrowbody production has recovered much more strongly.

“The supply of new long-haul aircraft is likely to remain relatively constrained for some time,” he observes. As such, airlines may need to keep older widebody aircraft in service for longer than they had originally planned – which supports continued refurbishment demand.

“Even as overall aircraft deliveries improve, I would therefore expect the refurbishment cycle for widebodies to remain fairly resilient until production normalises meaningfully,” says Sum.

Adds Bauer: “The 777-9 delays have forced carriers like Emirates and SIA to keep existing widebodies competitive for longer. Even when deliveries normalise, refurbishment is cyclical rather than one-off. The volume may flatten in the early 2030s, but it won’t disappear.

“Retrofit is now a permanent part of fleet strategy, not a stopgap.”

And, as SIA gears up to unveil new cabin products next month, Singapore’s flag carrier will soon be joining a crowded fray of in-flight interior upgraders.

data.title: US business activity expands, prices surge by most since 2022
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] US business activity grew at a slightly slower pace in October but remained close to a multi-year high as robust demand pushed new orders, employment and prices higher.

The S&P Global flash composite index fell 0.8 point to 57.6 in October, data released on Friday (Oct 23) showed. That was the second-highest reading since 2022. Figures above 50 indicate expansion.

A gauge of selling prices rose at the fastest pace in more than four years, reflecting a sharp rise in the cost of energy, transportation and raw materials.

“Cost pressures remain a key concern, notably as the renewed surge in oil prices reverberates through to impact a wide variety of goods and services,” Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said.

Bottlenecks are also getting worse. Supplier delivery times lengthened the most since 2022, with S&P Global citing material and labour shortages, as well as overloaded suppliers and shipping delays.

Even so, Williamson said that, outside the pandemic reopening, US businesses are enjoying their strongest period of growth since 2015.

Strong consumer spending, artificial intelligence-fuelled investment and defence outlays have all bolstered US businesses this year. New orders, a gauge of demand, posted the fastest growth in four-and-a-half years in October.

Companies are responding by adding more workers. The composite index for employment was the second-highest in four years, and the manufacturing index showed factory headcount advancing at the fastest pace since 2012.

Looking ahead, investment in AI and related technologies is anticipated to support demand and the broader economy next year, too.

Forecasters raised their estimates for private investment growth in the third quarter and in all of 2027 in the latest Bloomberg News survey of economists.

The group’s overall manufacturing index inched up to 56, the strongest since May 2022, while a gauge of activity at service providers eased. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Stocks to watch: FCT, Olam, OUE Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 22):

Frasers Centrepoint Trust (FCT): The trust posted a distribution per unit (DPU) of S$0.06214 for the second half ended September, up 2.6 per cent from S$0.06059 in the previous corresponding period. This raised total DPU for FY2026 to S$0.1235 – a new high. Revenue for H2 was up 8.7 per cent at S$223 million, and net property income rose 11.5 per cent to S$160.9 million. The increases were driven by contributions from Northpoint City South Wing, as well as higher passing rents across most malls. Units of FCT ended Wednesday 1 per cent or S$0.02 higher at S$2.06.

Olam Group : The group said on Wednesday that neither it nor Olam Agri owns or operates oil palm plantations or concessions in Indonesia. As a result, neither has direct operational exposure to recent forest and peatland fires. It added that Olam Agri ceased to be its subsidiary in April. The group was responding to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation and said it was unaware of any formal regulatory inquiries or notices relating to Indonesian forest fires contributing to haze. Shares of Olam rose S$0.01 or 1.1 per cent to S$0.91 before the announcement.

OUE Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : It posted a 4.6 per cent year-on-year increase in net property income to S$59.6 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, as stronger hospitality performance offset weaker contributions from its commercial portfolio. Revenue rose 3.1 per cent to S$72.6 million while financing costs fell 12.4 per cent year on year to S$18.9 million, the Reit manager. Units of OUE Reit shed S$0.01 or 2.9 per cent to S$0.33 on Wednesday.

data.title: Tech sell-off relents, oil at five-month high
data.description:
[LONDON] The rout in global tech shares eased on Friday after fears over the vast funding needs of artificial intelligence hammered Wall Street and triggered the biggest rally in US Treasuries in more than three years.

Asia’s bourses steadied overnight and, though Europe was 0.5 per cent lower ahead of Wall Street’s open, there was some respite from the pressure on French government bonds , where widening spreads had drawn comparisons with the eurozone debt crisis.

Oil, however, showed no signs of easing, with Brent at a new five-month peak of US$115 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and reports that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections.

European natural gas prices jumped another 4 per cent too, leaving them almost 30 per cent higher so far in October.

“It’s certainly a nervy market,” said Societe Generale’s global head of currency strategy, Kit Juckes.

“The oil price is just grinding higher... and we’ve got an inevitable correction in tech after its huge run-up, so it’s actually hard to see why the US dollar isn’t higher.”

The US currency was 0.2 per cent stronger on the day against its main basket of other top currencies, but it remains flat for the week.

The euro, meanwhile, was headed for a moderate weekly loss, which was not a big move, Juckes added, given all the bond market risk. The yen was on track for its biggest weekly rise in over a month after attracting safe-haven demand.

Focus on the futures

For the jittery Wall Street bulls, Nasdaq futures were off 0.5 per cent, while S&P 500 futures slipped 0.25 per cent after the Nasdaq’s 2.6 per cent tumble on Thursday, its biggest slump since June.

Telecommunications stocks were the latest casualties after a report that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was in talks to launch a nationwide cellphone carrier, sending AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile down more than 4 per cent in premarket trading.

Thursday’s rout had the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, the companies of which are at the centre of the AI boom, plunging almost 7 per cent. The likes of Meta dropped nearly 8 per cent, whilst CoreWeave’s share price slumped 10 per cent amid concerns about its debt burden.

Back in the bond markets, US Treasury yields were ticking up again, but were still just about under the key 5 per cent level after Thursday’s run for safety had fuelled their biggest one-day drop since March 2023.

Markets have also started paring back bets on global interest rate hikes. Almost a full quarter-point US Fed rate hike for next year has been stripped out this week amid the concerns over AI.

A December US Federal Reserve hike is no longer fully priced either, with the implied probability falling to 85 per cent.

In Europe, too, the chance of a European Central Bank December hike is down from 90 to 69 per cent earlier in the week, Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid pointed out.

French yields, which were down four basis points (bps) at 5.05 per cent, have risen nearly 27 bps this week, the most of any major eurozone country and the most in a week since late May.

The premium investors demand to hold French government debt over safe-haven German Bunds, dubbed “le spread”, remained above 170 after reaching its widest since the eurozone debt crisis, amid concerns over France’s finances and political uncertainty.

AI rally runs aground

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei dipped 0.3 per cent to end its week down over 4 per cent, while South Korea’s Kospi ended its session higher but after shedding as much as 4 per cent early on.

Mainland China’s blue chips found support after hitting their lowest since July 2025, with the CSI300 closing the day up 11.7 per cent. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng also rose 0.7 per cent after dropping 3 per cent on Thursday.

“It is hard to get too bearish on equities overall just yet, with earnings growth still positive and the hard economic data holding up well,” said Diana Mousina, deputy chief economist at AMP.

“All of this means that the AI trade isn’t necessarily over, but it is changing. It is no longer a case of ‘buy everything’.”

Gold failed to catch any safe-haven demand and was flat at $US$4,027 an ounce in London after a near 3 per cent drop on Thursday that leaves it down just over 3 per cent for the week. REUTERS

data.title: Oil tops US$115 to 5-month high as Middle East supply risks mount
data.description:
BRENT oil was trading at the highest level since May as attacks on Saudi Arabia intensified and the war with Iran remained unresolved.

The global benchmark traded around US$115 a barrel on Friday (Oct 23), up almost 4 per cent this week, while West Texas Intermediate was above US$100.

Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed recent attacks on the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, as well as deadly strikes on an oilfield and airport in the kingdom.

The flare-up threatens to widen hostilities around the Strait of Hormuz, where crude exports have recovered to near prewar levels.

Oil prices posted a sharp gain ahead of last weekend, as traders were reluctant to hold short positions while markets were closed. A similar pattern emerged on Friday.

At the White House on Thursday, President Donald Trump told reporters that the US has “knocked” out Iran and threatened to go “a little bit further”, without elaborating.

The New York Times reported this week that the US and Israel have developed plans for renewed strikes against the Islamic Republic after the American midterm elections early in November.

Brent is up more than 85 per cent in 2026 because of the US-Iran war, which is now approaching its ninth month.

Refined-product prices have risen even faster, most notably diesel. More recently, however, flows through Hormuz have surged, weighing on physical markets even as futures climb.

“One of the most frequent questions during our client meetings was why oil prices remain elevated despite the apparent recovery in Arab Gulf exports,” Citigroup analysts wrote in a note.

“We would caution against extrapolating a few days of stronger flows into a full normalisation of exports, as temporary increases may reflect inventory drawdowns or the release of previously hoarded barrels.”

The US is preparing for a protracted conflict with Iran and could still be mired in a stalemate a year from now, Trump’s ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told the Financial Times. The US Navy can maintain its blockade of Iranian ports for the “foreseeable future” and the administration is tightening economic pressure on Teheran, he added.

The Yemen-based Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent months.

State-owned Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters on Thursday and asked staff to work from home after an alarm, said people familiar with the matter. The reason for the alarm was not immediately known.

While crude flows from the Persian Gulf have recovered, oil-product shipments from the region remain constrained.

That squeeze, along with intensifying Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, has prompted governments to tap stockpiles. Trump is also pushing measures to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with Moscow. BLOOMBERG
